claims.text: As-received commercial Q235 steel has a naturally formed thin iron-oxide surface film.
The initial Q235 microstructure is unmodified.
At room temperature, slow oxidation produces a thin, compact Fe-oxide layer on Q235 steel.
A thin, compact Fe-oxide layer passivates Q235 steel at room temperature.
The room-temperature oxide remains stable and protective during aggressive NaCl exposure.
Room-temperature NaCl exposure causes minimal mass loss and degradation in Q235 steel.
Exposure of Q235 steel to aggressive salt at 700–900 °C accelerates oxide growth.
High-temperature salt exposure transforms the Q235 surface oxide into a thicker oxide layer.
The oxide formed on Q235 steel under high-temperature salt exposure is more porous than the room-temperature oxide.
The oxide formed on Q235 steel under high-temperature salt exposure is less adherent than the room-temperature oxide.
Rapid high-temperature oxidation increases grain-boundary diffusion in the oxide.
Increased oxide porosity and poor interfacial adhesion cause oxide spallation.
Oxide spallation accelerates corrosion of Q235 steel.
High-temperature salt-exposed Q235 steel will exhibit greater corrosion rates than the room-temperature salt-exposed reference.
High-temperature salt-exposed Q235 steel will exhibit greater mass loss than the room-temperature salt-exposed reference.
Oxide thickness, porosity, and adhesion mediate whether the steel surface retains corrosion protection.
A dense ZrTiO4 surface oxide formed after annealing an AlCrTiZrMo HEA film at 800 °C for 1 hour prevents continued oxidation.
An AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 hour has strong tribocorrosion resistance associated with a stable dense microstructure and favorable mechanical properties.
Pretreatment, coating, or alloying that significantly changes oxide-formation kinetics may prevent the proposed mechanism from applying.
Minor alloying elements may affect oxide properties and the critical temperature for degradation in Q235 steel.

contradictions.description: The intervention calls for testing samples with and without prior annealing, whereas the stated initial state and falsification design specify only as-received, unmodified samples and do not define an annealed arm.
